description: Hey! I’m Ron, a CS student at Lincoln University (Class of 2028) focused on backend and cloud. I build with Python, Java, Go, and Linux. Recent projects include a mini container runtime in Go, an AWS WordPress/RDS lab, and PGH Transit, a real-time bus tracker from Steel Hacks. I’m looking for teammates with any skills or new to a hackathon. All experience levels are welcome. I want everyone to contribute and build something people actually use!
summary:
We built the Crew Health Distress Simulator, health monitoring software for astronauts on long missions far from Earth. It streams five vital signs every second (heart rate, breathing rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature and a stress score) and compares each reading with that astronaut’s own normal, not one fixed alarm line. A heart rate of 70 is ordinary for one crew member and a warning sign for an athlete whose resting rate is 50, so a personal baseline catches problems a standard monitor would miss.

When readings drift, the alert rises from Watch to Caution to Emergency, and an action guide unlocks. An Earth-delay switch means Mission Control’s answer arrives too late, so the crew must act on its own, the self-sufficiency NASA’s Human Research Program names as essential for deep space. An onboard health assistant answers basic health and distress questions offline, and a debrief scores how fast the crew detected and responded.

Each emergency scenario is built on a named NASA spaceflight risk, letting crews train before launch and test the detector safely.
details:
What it does. The Crew Health Distress Simulator monitors an astronaut’s vital signs, decides when something is wrong, and guides the crew through the response when Earth cannot help in time. The home screen is a board of cards, one per vital sign plus the crew member, Mission Control, the alert, the action guide, a health assistant and the debrief. Clicking any card opens a detail page with a live chart.

How it works. Each crew member has their own normal for every signal: an average and a usual spread. The detector scores each new reading as (value minus their average) divided by their spread, smooths out noise over the last 3 readings, and sets the alert level. One signal 2 spreads away is Watch, two signals is Caution, and any signal 3 spreads away, or a fast blood-oxygen drop, is Emergency. The scenario engine pushes readings through onset, escalation and peak. Right steps from the action guide bring them back to normal, while wrong or late steps make them worse.

Benefits and impact. A personal baseline catches dangerous changes that a one-size-fits-all alarm misses, and avoids false alarms for crew whose normal is simply different. Because the detector uses clear rules rather than a black box, the crew can see exactly why each alert fired. The simulator lets crews rehearse emergencies before launch and lets engineers test the detector safely without real astronaut data, which is protected for privacy. The data format matches signals that astronaut wearables record, so real crew data could plug in.

Tools. HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with no framework and no server, hosted on GitHub Pages. Charts are drawn by hand as SVG. Git and GitHub for teamwork: each of our four members owned separate files, connected through an agreed interface.

Creativity. The Earth-delay switch turns a health dashboard into a deep-space problem: the crew must act before Mission Control can answer. The onboard health assistant works offline, so it still helps when Earth is out of reach.

Factors we considered. All data is simulated and clearly labeled on screen. Every scenario is tied to a named risk from NASA’s Human Research Program: panic (behavioral health), cabin CO2 buildup (hostile and closed environments) and low blood oxygen (hypoxia). Alert levels are written in words as well as colors, so they’re readable by people who can’t tell the colors apart.
